newsitem.title: UK: British shares set to skid, not crash on U.S slide.
newsitem.headline: British shares set to skid, not crash on U.S slide.

text.p: British shares were lower at midday on Monday amid investor fears the London market would follow Wall Street's plunge last Friday.

But despite predictions that the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which has slid nearly 700 points or 10 percent over the past month, could lose another 10-15 percent before investors pluck up the courage to buy again, British shares are not expected to slavishly follow the U.S. market lower.
Friday's 148-point loss on the Dow, the eighth biggest drop in history for the index of 30-leading U.S. shares, pushed the FTSE 100 Index 30.9 points down to 4,239.8 on Monday.
But dealers noted that U.S. shares had soared by a whopping 70 percent over the past two years while British shares had "only" managed a 40 percent advance.
"After the huge rise on Wall Street the FTSE should outperform going down but you can't ignore what is going on in the U.S.," one senior share trader said.
"We can't have Wall Street going into freefall without the FTSE reacting."
The FTSE has so far reacted to the Dow's 10 percent decline over the past month by dropping just under five percent from its all time high of 4,444.3, reached on March 11.

Kirit Shah, share strategist at Japanese investment bank Sanwa International, who expects the Dow to drop at least another 10 percent in the coming weeks, believes the FTSE's reaction will be modest by comparison.
"The FTSE isn't as overvalued as the Dow so I wouldn't look for more than a five percent correction from current levels," Shah said.

Shah said both the U.S. and British share markets had risen sharply over the past few years as lower interest rates encouraged investors, many planning for their future retirement, to seek investments that could offer higher returns than a bank or building society account.

There are signs that the tidal wave of money may be dissipating in the United States as U.S. interest rates rise, making risky shares a less attractive investment than safe bank accounts where savings rates are rising.
But a flood of windfalls from forthcoming building society flotations should help keep the British cash wave from ending up on the rocks over the next few months.
"All of this new cash should help stabilise the FTSE," Shah said.

The Alliance & Leicester, one of Britain's traditional home loan providers, is due to be listed on the London Stock Exchange on April 21 followed by similar listings by four other building societies, including the Halifax, the nation's biggest, over the next few months.

Millions of eligible investing and borrowing members of the converting societies will receive free shares and many are expected to plough the cash, which could be in excess of 1,000 pounds ($1,620) per member, back into the stock market.

Technical analysts, strategists who believe history repeats itself in share dealings and use mathematics to support their theories, believe the FTSE could head lower than the 4,000 level predicted by Sanwa's Shah, however.
According to these analysts who ignore things like windfall cash floods, the FTSE is now in the first major corrective phase following an uptrend which has lasted two years.
Their calculations agree with Shah's initial prediction of a further five percent setback.

Like Shah, they predict the FTSE will find some buyers surfacing when it reaches the 4,000 level and that the buying will continue until June. But a final onslaught of selling should wipe another seven percent or so off the FTSE during the summer.
With this scenario, the current downtrend should be complete by September and the FTSE will have bottomed out at about 3,760 after having lost around 15 percent from its March 11 peak.
Traditionally the London share market begins an end of year rally in the autumn and, if the technical analysts are right, history could then repeat itself once again. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
